items.title: Navy rescues hijacked vessel with Iran crew, IAF lends helping hand
items.where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Amrita Nayak Dutta)
items.syllabus: GS3 › Security challenges and their management in border areas (maritime security); Various security forces and their mandate · GS2 › India's bilateral relations (Iran); Effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (West Asia) · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
items.summary: The Indian Navy, backed by an IAF C-17 airdrop of Marine Commandos, freed the fishing vessel Azini and its 20 Iranian crew, hijacked by pirates off Somalia last month, in an operation of over 48 hours.
ideas: Piracy as a regional threat: the Navy saw the hijacked vessel as a likely 'mother ship' for launching pirate attacks on merchant shipping, so freeing it protects the sea lanes as well as the crew.
GS3 · Maritime security
Hijacked fishing vessels used as pirate mother ships make piracy a threat to the whole sea lane, not to one crew.
Jointness in action: a mission-deployed warship, a maritime reconnaissance aircraft and Marine Commandos airdropped by an IAF C-17 worked together.
GS3 · Security forces and their mandate
The Azini rescue shows inter-service jointness turning surveillance into swift action at sea.
Restraint as strategy: after persistent surveillance, the Navy used 'calibrated non-kinetic measures' to contain the vessel before its tactical intervention, and all 20 crew were released.
GS3 · Maritime security / GS4 · Proportionality
Calibrated, non-kinetic force secured the hostages' release without escalation: security achieved with restraint.
First responder and preferred security partner: the Navy framed the operation as proof of India's role in the Indian Ocean Region, regardless of the crew's nationality.
GS2 · India and the IOR / GS3 · Security
Rescuing foreign crews builds India's credibility as the Indian Ocean's first responder and preferred security partner.
Diplomacy through rescue: Iran's Embassy praised India's HADR commitment and called the rescue a testament to Iran–India friendship and cooperation.
GS2 · India–Iran relations
Maritime help to Iranian sailors turns hard naval capability into soft-power goodwill with Iran.
keywords: A captured vessel used by pirates as a floating base to attack ships far from shore
Captured mother ships let pirates strike far out at sea, so freeing them is preventive security.
Using surveillance, blocking and pressure instead of firepower
GS3 · Security / GS4 · Ethics of force
Non-kinetic containment let the Navy secure the crew while keeping force to the minimum.
A country others in a region turn to first for maritime help
Every rescue at sea strengthens India's claim to be the Indian Ocean's preferred security partner.
A state whose capabilities provide security for the wider region, not only itself
Anti-piracy operations for other nations' crews show India acting as a net security provider.
HADR operations let India's armed forces win friends without firing a shot.
examples: Rescue of the Iranian crew of the Azini
Navy and IAF free 20 Iranian fishermen from pirates
GS4
GS3 · Maritime security · GS2 · India–Iran · GS4 · Compassion beyond borders
India's rescue of 20 Iranian fishermen shows that compassion and duty at sea do not depend on the victim's nationality.
Navy–IAF airdrop of Marine Commandos
C-17 precision airdrop to a vessel far at sea
GS3 · Security forces · jointness
The C-17 airdrop of Marine Commandos is a ready example of jointness among the armed forces.
Calibrated force against pirates
Surveillance and non-kinetic containment before intervention
GS4
GS3 · Security · GS4 · Means and ends · Essay
Containing pirates without escalation shows that the most effective use of power is often the most restrained.
pyqs: Why maritime security is vital for India's sea trade; challenges and way forward.
Maritime security challenges and India's organisational, technical and procedural initiatives.
IPMDA as a bridge between SAGAR and the Quad's Indo-Pacific strategy.
Role of the IMO in the marine environment and maritime safety and security.
IMO's shift of the piracy high-risk area in the Arabian Sea and India's concerns.

trend.t: Maritime questions began with a narrow piracy-zone issue (2014), widened to India's overall maritime security architecture (2022) and the link between security and sea trade (2025). In 2023 and 2026 the frame moved to institutions and partnerships: the IMO, then IPMDA, SAGAR and the Quad.
trend.watch: Maritime security has been asked in 2022, 2023, 2025 and 2026, so it is a must-study area. Questions now ask how India secures the seas through partnerships, not only its own navy.
focus: Threats at sea: piracy, attacks on shipping, chokepoints
India's institutions and initiatives for maritime security
SAGAR and India as a first responder in the IOR

potential: "The Indian Navy's role in the Indian Ocean Region is shifting from guarding India's coasts to securing the region's sea lanes." Discuss. (15 marks)
Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) has become a tool of India's maritime diplomacy. Examine with examples. (10 marks)
What challenges does the resurgence of piracy and attacks on merchant shipping pose to India's sea trade? Suggest measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: "The Indian Navy's role in the Indian Ocean Region is shifting from guarding India's coasts to securing the region's sea lanes." Discuss.

answer.t: In November 2026 the Indian Navy freed the Iranian fishing vessel Azini and its 20 crew from pirates, calling itself the 'first responder and preferred security partner' in the IOR.

pts.t: The Navy now acts against pirates far from India's coast because piracy threatens the sea lanes that carry India's trade.
pts.ex: Freeing the Azini, which could have been used as a pirate mother ship (2026).

pts.k: Protecting the shipping of all nations
pts.t: Rescues are carried out irrespective of the flag or the crew's nationality, building trust across the region.
pts.ex: 20 Iranian crew rescued; Iran's Embassy thanked India.

pts.t: Warships are kept on station in key areas round the year, so the Navy can respond quickly to incidents.
pts.ex: A mission-deployed warship intervened in the Azini rescue.

pts.t: Joint operations with the IAF extend the Navy's reach far out to sea.
pts.ex: Marine Commandos airdropped by an IAF C-17.

pts.t: Surveillance and information sharing let the Navy track threats across the region.
pts.ex: Information Fusion Centre – IOR at Gurugram; IPMDA with the Quad.

pts.t: Relief missions make India the first responder in crises across the IOR.
pts.ex: Operation Samudra Setu (2020) brought Indians home by sea during Covid.

pts.t: Attacks on merchant shipping in West Asia show how exposed India's trade and seafarers remain.
pts.ex: Indian-flagged sailing vessels attacked off Oman during the West Asia war (IE, 4 Nov 2026).

pts.t: The Navy's ships and aircraft are stretched across a huge ocean.
China's growing presence, including its base at Djibouti, competes for influence.
Fishing boats and sailing cargo vessels are hard to track and protect.
Sharing intelligence and responsibility with littoral states and partners is still uneven.
Prosecuting captured pirates across jurisdictions remains difficult, though India enacted the Maritime Anti-Piracy Act in 2022.
More ships, maritime patrol aircraft and unmanned systems for persistent watch.
Strengthen IFC-IOR and IPMDA links with littoral states.
Train and equip smaller IOR navies and coast guards under SAGAR.
Advisories, tracking and insurance support for small Indian vessels in risky waters.
Apply the Maritime Anti-Piracy Act and work through the IMO for common rules.
Continue non-kinetic, proportionate methods that resolve crises without escalation.
pts.ex: The Azini rescue.

answer.t: From the Azini rescue to HADR missions, India's Navy is becoming the IOR's first responder; capacity and partnerships will decide how far that role can grow.

items.title: On Govt agenda: New Rs 2,800-cr capex scheme for critical minerals
items.where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Pratyush Deep), with an Explained box
items.syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effects on industrial growth; Infrastructure: energy; Mobilisation of resources · GS1 › Distribution of key natural resources across the world and India · GS2 › Effect of policies of other countries on India's interests (China) · GS4 › Ethical issues in international relations
items.summary: The Union Cabinet is likely to take up a scheme of about Rs 2,800 crore that offers a 30% capital subsidy for two lithium and two nickel processing plants, to build India's domestic critical mineral processing base.
evolution: PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity goal; storage needs batteries (energy thread).
Cabinet to consider a capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing.
ideas: The gap is processing, not only mining: India has little processing capacity and is almost fully import-dependent for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
GS3 · Industry / GS1 · Resources
India's critical mineral weakness lies in processing; mining ore is of little use without the capacity to refine it.
Concentration as a strategic risk: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions, leaving India open to supply disruptions.
GS2 · India–China / GS3 · Economy
China's hold over mineral processing turns supply chains into tools of pressure, so diversification is national security.
Capex support to start a domestic base: a 30% capital subsidy for four plants (two lithium, two nickel) aims to turn ores into high-purity compounds, with cobalt recovered from nickel.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Capital subsidies for processing plants target the costliest, riskiest link in India's mineral value chain.
Clean-energy and strategic sectors depend on it: the minerals feed electric mobility, battery storage, electronics, defence and speciality steel.
GS3 · Energy / Defence industry
Without lithium, nickel and cobalt, India's EV and battery ambitions rest on imported inputs.
Cluster approach: processing parks in four states, each built as an ecosystem for one mineral, backed by a planned stockpile under the National Critical Minerals Mission.
GS1 · Location of industries / GS3 · Industrial policy
Mineral-specific parks link resource geography to industry, and a strategic stockpile insures against shocks.
keywords: Refining ores into high-purity chemicals used by battery and electronics makers
India's critical mineral challenge is mid-stream: refining, not just mining.
Using dominance over a resource to pressure other countries
China's control of mineral processing shows how supply chains can be weaponised in trade disputes.
A government reserve held to ride out supply disruptions
A critical mineral stockpile works like a strategic oil reserve for the battery age.
Building each stage of production at home
Localising the mineral value chain cuts import dependence from mine to battery.
Industrial parks placed near the raw material they use
Odisha's nickel and Gujarat's heavy rare earths show resource-based clustering in practice.
data: Allocation committed for a National Critical Mineral Stockpile Programme, 2024-25 to 2030-31
National Critical Minerals Mission (Government of India), via IE
The government has committed Rs 500 crore (2024-25 to 2030-31) for a critical mineral stockpile under the NCMM.
examples: Four mineral-specific processing parks
Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh for rare earths, Odisha for nickel, Maharashtra for lithium
GS1 · Distribution of resources · GS3 · Industrial policy
Matching parks to state resources (Odisha's nickel, Gujarat's heavy rare earths) is a model of resource-based industrialisation.
China's leverage over mineral processing
Dominance used as leverage in trade tensions
GS4
GS2 · India–China · GS3 · Economy · GS4 · Ethics in IR
China's use of mineral processing as leverage is a clear example of economic interdependence turned into coercion.
Odisha as a gateway for imported nickel
Eastern location suits imports from Indonesia
GS1 · Location of industries · GS2 · Act East
Odisha's eastern coast lets India process nickel imported from Indonesia, linking resources to the Act East region.
pyqs: The West fostering India as an alternative to China's supply chains.
Challenges for India as the world moves from free trade to protectionism; how to meet them.
Rationale, achievements and improvements of the PLI scheme.
Why India's mining contributes little to GDP despite its Gondwana origin.
Why mining is an environmental hazard; remedial measures.

trend.t: Mineral questions began in physical geography (resource distribution, mining's low GDP share, 2017–2022) and industrial location (2019, 2020). From 2024 the frame shifted to supply chains and geopolitics: India as an alternative to China (2024), protectionism and industrial incentives such as PLI (2025).
trend.watch: Supply-chain resilience and China-plus-one questions are rising since 2024, while mining's environmental cost was asked again in 2025. Critical minerals sit where these meet, so expect a direct question soon.
focus: Industrial policy tools: PLI, capex subsidies, parks
Resource geography and location of processing
Environmental cost of mining and processing

potential: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains. (15 marks)
Why has India remained import-dependent for critical minerals despite its resource base? Examine the role of processing capacity. (10 marks)
How can mineral-specific processing parks promote regional industrial development in India? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Critical minerals are to the 21st century what oil was to the 20th." Discuss India's vulnerabilities and the steps needed to secure its critical mineral supply chains.

answer.t: In November 2026 the Union Cabinet is set to consider a Rs 2,800-crore capex scheme for lithium and nickel processing, as India remains almost fully import-dependent for key critical minerals.

pts.t: Lithium, nickel and cobalt are core to Li-ion batteries for EVs and grid storage.
pts.ex: Needed for India's 500 GW non-fossil goal.

pts.t: Smartphones, semiconductors and electronics depend on these minerals.
Defence systems and speciality steels need rare earths and alloys.
Like oil, control of supply gives power over others.
pts.ex: China's processing dominance used in trade tensions.

pts.t: India relies almost completely on imports for cobalt, lithium, nickel, rare earths and silicon.
Even where ore exists, India lacks refining capacity to make battery-grade compounds.
Global processing is concentrated in China, which has curbed exports of some minerals in the past.
pts.ex: Export curbs on gallium and germanium (2023).

pts.t: Large parts of India's mineral potential remain unexplored.
Processing plants are costly and technology-intensive, deterring private investment.
Mining and chemical processing can damage land, water and local communities.
30% capital subsidy for lithium and nickel plants under the proposed scheme.
pts.ex: Rs 500–900 crore cap per beneficiary.

pts.t: A mission-mode approach to exploration, processing and overseas assets, with a planned stockpile.
pts.ex: Rs 500 crore committed for stockpiling (2024-25 to 2030-31).

pts.t: Ecosystems in four states matched to their resources.
pts.ex: Odisha for nickel, Gujarat and AP for rare earths.

pts.t: Secure supplies abroad through state firms and partners.
pts.ex: KABIL; India's membership of the Minerals Security Partnership.

pts.t: Recover minerals from used batteries and e-waste to reduce fresh demand.
Strict environmental norms and benefit-sharing with mining communities.
pts.ex: District Mineral Foundations.

answer.t: Just as oil security shaped the last century, building domestic processing, diverse partners and a strategic stockpile will decide India's energy and strategic autonomy in this one.

items.title: KPSC scam: ED says ex-chairman building Rs 35-cr 'dream project'
items.syllabus: GS2 › Constitutional bodies (State Public Service Commissions, Art. 315); Role of civil services in a democracy; Transparency and accountability · GS4 › Probity in governance; Integrity; Conflict of interest
items.summary: The ED told a special court that former KPSC chairman Shivashankarappa Sahukar, arrested in a veterinary doctors' recruitment scam, was building a Rs 35-crore complex; the Karnataka HC has reconstituted the SIT probing the scam.
evolution: NTA overhaul: 5,000 experts empanelled to set and vet papers (exam integrity).
KPSC ex-chairman accused of selling answer keys; HC reconstitutes SIT.
ideas: Capture at the top: the chairman and a member of a constitutional recruiting body are accused of leaking answer keys to nine aspirants for bribes, with the exam controller, an IAS officer, also implicated.
GS2 · Constitutional bodies / GS4 · Probity
When those who guard merit sell it, the corruption is institutional, not individual.
A pattern, not a lapse: aspirants flagged withheld marks, manipulated interview panels, altered tabulation records, tampered answer sheets and leaked papers.
GS2 · Recruitment and civil services
Recruitment fraud runs through every stage, from paper-setting to interviews, so reform must cover the whole chain.
Conflict of interest: the chairman was suspended in a separate case of illegal recruitment of his own daughter by the KPSC.
GS4 · Conflict of interest
Hiring one's own relative through the body one heads is the textbook case of conflict of interest.
Political cover weakens independence: the IE found the chairman was handpicked by one party in 2019 and shielded by the next government after 2023.
GS2 · Independence of constitutional bodies
Bipartisan protection of a compromised appointee shows why PSC appointments need insulation from politics.
Accountability through many agencies: ED under the PMLA, the CID and a court-monitored SIT probe the case, and the HC kept CID officers out of the new SIT.
GS2 · Accountability / Judiciary
Court-monitored probes help restore credibility when investigating agencies themselves face doubts.
keywords: Paper leaks replace meritocracy with a market where public posts go to the highest bidder.
Control of an independent body by private or partisan interests
Political patronage of PSC chiefs risks institutional capture of recruitment.
Money gained through a criminal act, the basis of action under the PMLA
The ED treats bribe money from recruitment as proceeds of crime under the PMLA.
The chairman's suspension for his daughter's selection is a clear case of nepotism.
examples: KPSC veterinary doctors' recruitment scam
Answer keys allegedly sold by the PSC chairman and a member
GS4
GS2 · State PSCs · GS4 · Probity and integrity
The KPSC scam shows how corruption at the top of a recruiting body betrays every honest aspirant.
PSC chief's daughter recruited
Chairman suspended over his own daughter's selection
GS4
GS4 · Conflict of interest · nepotism
A recruiting body's head selecting his own daughter is a ready example of conflict of interest.
Court-monitored SIT
Karnataka HC reconstitutes the SIT and keeps CID officers out
GS2 · Judiciary · accountability
The HC's control over the SIT is an example of the judiciary protecting the credibility of an investigation.
pyqs: Aims of the Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.
Public perception of civil servants' integrity in democratic governance.
Transparency and accountability as building stakeholders' trust.
Institutional quality and civil service reform.

trend.t: Civil service questions moved from structure (cadre system 2014, neutrality 2017) to institutional quality (2020) and public trust in civil servants' integrity (2024). In 2024 UPSC also asked directly about the law against unfair means in public examinations, and in 2026 about transparency building trust.
trend.watch: The integrity of public recruitment is now tested directly, as the 2024 question on the Public Examination Act showed. Prepare paper leaks, PSC independence and trust in institutions.
focus: Integrity of public examinations and laws against leaks

potential: "Recurring recruitment scams in State Public Service Commissions threaten both meritocracy and public trust." Discuss and suggest reforms. (15 marks)
Examine the constitutional safeguards for the independence of State Public Service Commissions. Are they adequate? (10 marks)
What is conflict of interest? Illustrate with an example from public recruitment and suggest how it can be prevented. (10 marks, GS4)

practice.q: "Recurring recruitment scams in State Public Service Commissions threaten both meritocracy and public trust." Discuss and suggest reforms.
parts: How scams threaten meritocracy and trust

answer.t: In November 2026 the ED told a court that former KPSC chairman Shivashankarappa Sahukar, accused of selling answer keys, was building a Rs 35-crore complex: the guardian of merit stands accused of selling it.

answer.h: How scams threaten meritocracy and trust

pts.t: Leaked papers and answer keys hand posts to those who pay, not those who perform.
pts.ex: Bribes for answer keys in the KPSC veterinary officers' exam.

pts.t: Years of preparation by honest candidates are wasted, hurting the young and the poor most.
Officers selected through bribes may treat office as a means to recover their investment.
Each scam makes citizens doubt every result, even honest ones.
Cancelled exams and court cases freeze recruitment for years.
Frustration among unemployed youth can turn into protest and alienation.
Members are often chosen for loyalty, not integrity, and then shielded.
pts.ex: KPSC chief handpicked in 2019, shielded after 2023 (IE).

pts.t: Relatives of insiders sit the very exams the body conducts.
pts.ex: KPSC chairman suspended over his daughter's recruitment.

pts.t: Manual tabulation, discretionary interviews and poor custody of papers invite tampering.
pts.ex: Altered tabulation records, manipulated interview panels.

pts.t: Members, exam controllers and middlemen work together.
pts.ex: IAS exam controller also implicated.

pts.t: Multiple agencies and long trials weaken deterrence.
pts.ex: ED, CID and a reconstituted SIT in the KPSC case.

pts.t: Members can be removed only on a reference to the Supreme Court under Article 317, so action is slow.
Fix eligibility and integrity criteria and use a selection committee for PSC members.
Encrypted digital papers, CCTV custody chains and computer-based tests.
Reduce interview weightage, use mixed panels and record proceedings.
Apply the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 model and similar state laws, with fast-track courts.
Compulsory disclosure and recusal where a relative is a candidate.
Publish answer keys and marks, and allow time-bound challenges.

answer.t: A PSC's legitimacy rests on its integrity; insulating appointments and making every stage of recruitment transparent is the only way to restore faith in merit.

ethics.title: Rescue beyond borders
ethics.news: The Indian Navy and IAF freed 20 Iranian fishermen from pirates, using calibrated non-kinetic measures; Iran called it a testament to friendship.
ethics.syllabus: Ethical issues in international relations; Compassion; Means and ends (use of force)
ethics.link: Saving foreign sailors shows that duty to human life does not stop at nationality, and choosing calibrated, minimum force shows that even security operations can be guided by proportionality. Ethics here also serves interest: compassion builds trust between nations.
ethics.question: "Humanitarian action can be the meeting point of ethics and national interest in international relations." Discuss with examples.

ethics.title: When supply chains become weapons
ethics.news: China dominates global critical mineral processing and has used it as leverage in trade tensions; India plans a scheme to build its own processing base.
ethics.syllabus: Ethical issues in international relations; Environmental ethics
ethics.link: Using control over resources the whole world needs to coerce others turns interdependence into a weapon, raising a question of fairness between nations. As India builds its own base, it also owes a duty to its mineral regions: self-reliance should not come at the cost of land, water and local communities.
ethics.question: Is it ethical for nations to use their control over critical resources as leverage in international relations? Discuss.

ethics.title: Selling the gate to public service
ethics.news: A former KPSC chairman, accused of leaking answer keys for bribes, was also suspended over the commission's recruitment of his own daughter.
ethics.syllabus: Probity in governance; Integrity; Conflict of interest; Impartiality
ethics.link: A recruiting body is the gate to public service: when its head sells answer keys and selects his own daughter, it betrays the impartiality and trust on which the whole civil service rests. Corruption at the entry point corrupts every service that follows.
ethics.question: "Corruption in public recruitment is the most damaging form of corruption because it corrupts the system at its source." Discuss.

essay.title: Pirates contained without escalation
essay.text: Freeing 20 Iranian fishermen from pirates, the Indian Navy first tracked the vessel and contained it with calibrated non-kinetic measures, then intervened swiftly; all the crew came home.
essay.use: For 'The supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting' (2025) and 'With greater power comes greater responsibility' (2014).

essay.title: Minerals as the new leverage
essay.text: China's dominance over critical mineral processing, used as leverage in trade tensions, shows that power between nations now flows through batteries and supply chains, not only armies.
essay.use: For 'Technology as the silent factor in international relations' (2020).
